chart.intro: The 文海 as a chart: each row is a rhyme with its tone, each column an initial group, and every character stands where the two meet. Hover a character for its fanqie, Tibetan gloss and meaning.
chart.legend: Hover a character for its fanqie, Tibetan gloss and meaning. Tibetan letters come from the British Library manuscripts and 李範文 (1994, pp. 270–281), with “?” where a letter could not be read. Group headings follow 孫伯君 (2017).
chart.chineseLegend: Press a boxed rhyme number to open the Chinese characters that transcribe that rhyme (郭抒遠 2019).
chart.chineseOpen: Show the Chinese characters that transcribe this rhyme
fanqie.inferred: No source gives this character a reading; inferred from the spelling it shares with {char}.

about.cangjieSource: rime_tangutcjkk by Hulenkius, the Tangut Cangjie scheme of Kawasaki Keigo (2016) for RIME: 11,805 full and short codes, components under codes beginning p. The table itself warns that some characters are wrongly encoded, and the repository states no licence. This is the repository’s 2026.02.02 revision: 4,725 of its 7,058 characters carry more than one code, because a glyph can be analysed more than one way, and every code is accepted and shown. A proposal to standardise the analyses that disagree with each other is still open upstream, so 250 characters hold no code that their parts alone would predict. Tutorial and practice tables: tlistlil.github.io/sps/Tang/cj.
about.rhymeBooks: Tangut-rhyme-dictionaries-data (西夏語韻書データ) by nkay0: each character’s rhyme class in the 文海, its tone, its initial group, and the two characters its fanqie is spelt from, taken from Han Xiaomang (2021) and the editions of the 文海, 文海寶韻, 同音 and 合編. The table’s own page and index numbers are not reproduced. The repository states no licence.
about.classNames: The 同音 names each of its nine initial classes in Tangut, 唇音重一品 for 重唇音一品 and so on; the chart takes them from table 2 of 孫伯君 (2017), 論西夏對漢語音韻學的繼承與創新. The 同音 calls the ninth class 來日音九品, where the 五音切韻 has 舌齒音.
about.tibetan: Index of Tangut Characters with Corresponding Tibetan Phonetic Glosses by Andrew West (BabelStone, 2011-12-19): 261 Tibetan glosses of 197 characters from five British Library manuscripts, Or.12380/1842, 3495, 3909, 3910 and 3911. The Chart page shows them under 194 of those characters; 𗤠 and 𘂧 have no place in the rhyme table and 𗈪 no rhyme number. The index omits some incomplete glosses, and warns that some glosses are hard to read, so it probably holds some erroneous readings; a “?” marks a letter it could not read. The page states no licence. The spellings at the foot of the Chart page’s cells are 李範文’s table (《宋代西北方音》, 1994, pp. 270–281), read from KwingiemChan’s repost on Zhihu and not checked against the book.
about.gong: With 龔煌城 chosen on the Chart page, each rhyme reads his per-character GHC value from the Tangut Pronunciation Database; where the records leave a rhyme without one, it falls back to his rhyme table (《西夏语概要》, 2005), from table 1-3-1 of 郭抒遠’s 2019 thesis, read from KwingiemChan’s scans on Zhihu and not checked against either book. Long vowels are written double, and rhyme 105 is printed jwa though other sources give it a final r. Rhyme 16 and a few marks too fine to read in the scan follow a second scanned table and other readings in the same system.
about.chinese: The Chinese characters under a rhyme on the Chart page come from table 1-3-1 of 郭抒遠’s 2019 thesis on the 黑水城 medical texts. The finals are 李範文’s (《宋代西北方音》, 1994), as paired with those characters in KwingiemChan’s article on Zhihu; neither book has been checked. A character the article left out or altered has no final, and 蓆, 苓, 芣 and 鰲 follow the article because the scan cannot tell them from 蒂, 芩, 苿 and 鳖.
about.downes: The row marked Downes on a card is Alan Downes’s English gloss from tangut.info, read from the copy in C27Ezx/TangutTranslator, which states an MIT licence. It is kept apart from Wiktionary’s meanings because the two can disagree: of 441 characters with both, 373 share a word. The site itself was offline when read on 2026-11-05.
about.leilinTitle: Chinese glosses from the 類林
about.leilin: The row marked 類林 on a card is the Chinese word used for the character in Guillaume Jacques’s Leilin database, read from tinbreaker/tangut-text. No licence is stated. Only characters that text uses have one, and some words are grammatical labels.
about.handsTitle: Tibetan and Sanskrit spellings by character
about.hands: The Tibetan spellings by hand class A–E and the Sanskrit on a character’s card come from scanned tables in KwingiemChan’s article on Zhihu, which does not name the study they reproduce. They were machine-read. Each row’s 李範文 number was checked against the rhyme, tone and initial class in the rhyme books, and rows that failed are left out unless a second source confirms them; 134 of the 151 characters also in BabelStone’s index share a spelling with it. The spellings have not been checked one by one against the scans. One Sanskrit form is read ñi where the machine gave the IPA letter ɲi. The tables print these in transliteration; the card converts them to Tibetan script and Devanagari, sets Wylie or IAST beside them, and gives IPA on hover. The IPA reads the letters one by one and is this site’s reading, not the source’s. A ? marks a letter that could not be read.
about.seta: A Tibetan spelling that matches a precomposed character of Tibetan Extension-A shows its private-use code on hover, and Find reads the same code. The mapping comes from Andrew West’s archived table, which states no licence; Set B was never published.
about.strokes: Ideographs from Unicode’s TangutSources.txt (Unicode 18.0); components counted from their glyphs in this project’s review.
about.identifiers: Li Fanwen 2008 numbers come from Unicode’s TangutSources.txt. 文海 positions come from Andrew West’s BabelStone lookup; the Mojikyo code points come from his Mojikyo converter and the XXZT code points from his XXZT converter. The BabelStone pages state no licence.
about.attestation: The corpus joins two kinds of record: an edition with facsimile and translation, and transcriptions from Wikisource. Each source keeps its own rights, shown beside its places and below.
about.attestCount: So far: {lines} lines from {sources} texts, {characters} characters, {distinct} distinct.
about.glyphs: Noto Serif Tangut (SIL OFL 1.1), from Google Fonts. The drawing pad’s glyph masks are rendered from the same font. Descriptions use a 2 KB subset of GenZui Sans for the sixteen ideographic description characters (SIL OFL 1.1).
about.howCangjie: A typed code lists every character whose full or short code begins with it: an exact code first, then shorter codes. Wrong codes in the table are found as the table has them.
about.howReading: Readings in the seven systems are folded to plain letters: diacritics dropped, IPA letters replaced by the nearest Latin letter (ɨ ɪ → i, ə → e, ŋ → ng), separators removed. A final digit is the tone. Near matches also ignore medial j and y and a prenasal before a stop. The search also answers one further system from CCAMC, and a result that only that match shows a CCAMC link instead of the reading.
about.howDraw: The drawing and each glyph are fitted into the same 32-pixel square by their longer side, the glyph reduced to a one-cell line along its pen, and compared by how far each line lies from the other’s and by the direction the ink runs at each point. Stroke order plays no part. On eighty characters drawn by one reader, the right character came first about four times in ten and within the first five about one time in two.
about.howParts: A character matches when the parts it holds at any layer include every chosen part, as often as chosen. A run of components that spells another character is read as that character in turn; the source descriptions are BabelStone's and use components only.
about.howAttest: A character outside the corpus has no attestation yet: the recorded texts are a small part of what survives, and absence says nothing about the character.
about.markText: 𘅤 (U+18164), glossed “to write” in Wiktionary, read rjar¹ by Li Fanwen.
about.kept: Every drawing made on the Draw page and every character picked from a finder is recorded with the finder it came from, the character chosen and the place it stood in the list. A drawing kept with a pick is one example the search could be measured or trained on. A record carries a random id that lives in your browser, never your address, and there is no account. The quiz saves the same fields for each round, with the prompt it asked for.
about.footer: Descriptions are also composed in the IDS Workshop, which runs on the same component data; its data notes give each file’s source and licence.

intro.title: The Tanguts and their script
intro.lead: The Tanguts (党項) were a people of what is now northwest China whose state, Western Xia (西夏, 1038–1227), made its own script; this page covers the people, the script, the language, the texts and the script today. [1][2]
intro.s1.heading: People and state
intro.s1.body:
In Chinese the Tanguts were Dǎngxiàng, in Tibetan Mi-nyag, in Old Turkic Taŋut and in Mongolian Tangud. The Turkic name is first recorded in the Orkhon inscriptions of 735. [2] The Tanguts were a federation of tribes. Their early home was the highlands of southeast Qinghai and northwest Sichuan, in the Amdo and Kham regions. [1][2]

The tribes lived first under Tuyuhun authority. Around 630 the Tuoba leader Tuoba Chici submitted to the Tang, which set up indirectly administered prefectures with local chiefs as prefects. [1][2] In the early 8th century pressure from the Tibetan Empire pushed the Tanguts north to the Ordos region. By the An Lushan rebellion (755–763) they were the leading local power in what is now eastern Gansu, Ningxia and northern Shaanxi. [1][2] In 881 the Tangut leader Li Sigong helped suppress the Huang Chao rebellion. The Tang court gave him the prefectures of Xia, Sui and Yin and the imperial surname Li. [1][2]

In 1038 Li Yuanhao (Emperor Jingzong) proclaimed the Western Xia state. The state called itself 白高大夏國 or 大白高國, “White High Great Xia”. Its capital was Xingqing, today Yinchuan. [1][2] The Mongols destroyed the state in 1227. [1][2][4]
intro.s2.heading: The script
intro.s2.body:
According to the History of Song, the official Yeli Renrong (野利仁榮) designed the script in 1036 in a short time, and schools were founded to teach it. [3] A 2004 count gives 5,863 characters, excluding variants. [3]

The characters look like Chinese characters and use the same kinds of strokes, but they are formed differently, and none are pictographic. [3] Many characters combine two components, the recurring parts from which characters are built; a few combine three or four. Each combination joins two elements of meaning, or one element of meaning and one of sound. [3] A component can carry the meaning or sound of another character that contains it. It can mean different things in different characters, and it can change shape with its position. [3][10] Regular, running, cursive and seal forms were used, as in Chinese calligraphy. [3]
intro.s3.heading: The language
intro.s3.body:
Tangut is a Sino-Tibetan language of the Tibeto-Burman branch. [4] It was long placed in the Qiangic or Yi groups. Since the 2010s it has been placed in West Gyalrongic, and Beaudouin (2023) argues that it belongs with Horpa. [4][6][7] Its roots were monosyllabic, and it had two tones, level and rising. The rhyme dictionaries arrange 105 rimes, the part of a syllable after its initial consonant. [4]

Only about 10% of Tangut characters carry a phonetic element, a figure given by Sofronov, against more than 90% in Chinese. The writing therefore gives little direct evidence of sound. [4] Reconstruction rests on three kinds of source: the Tangut–Chinese glossary Pearl in the Palm (番漢合時掌中珠), dated 1190; Tibetan transcriptions; and monolingual rhyme dictionaries, namely the Sea of Characters (文海), two editions of the Homophones (同音) and the 文海雜類. These dictionaries record pronunciation by fanqie, a method that spells a syllable with two other characters, one for its initial and one for its rime. [4]
intro.s4.heading: Texts and decipherment
intro.s4.body:
A large Buddhist canon, the collected scriptures, was translated from Tibetan and Chinese and printed in Tangut. Some of its compilations survive in no Chinese or Tibetan version. [3][4] Secular texts include law codes and a Tangut translation of the Art of War. [3][4] Most surviving texts were excavated at Khara-Khoto by Pyotr Kozlov in 1909. About 10,000 volumes from the 11th to the early 13th centuries, mostly Buddhist texts, law codes and legal documents, are in the Institute of Oriental Manuscripts of the Russian Academy of Sciences in St Petersburg. Smaller collections are in the British Library, the Bibliothèque nationale de France and libraries in Beijing. [4][8]

Decipherment began in the late 19th century with S. W. Bushell, Gabriel Devéria and Georges Morisse, who worked from coins, a bilingual stele at Wuwei and a Tangut Lotus Sutra. [4][9] Nikolai Nevsky compiled the first dictionary and reconstructed grammatical particles. His Tangut Philology appeared in 1960. Nishida, Kepping, Gong and Li Fanwen followed. [4][9]
intro.s5.heading: After 1227
intro.s5.body:
The script outlived the state. The last known text is on a pair of dharani pillars at Baoding, Hebei, erected in 1502; a dharani is a Buddhist incantation. [3][9]

Unicode, the standard for text on computers, encoded 6,881 Tangut characters in version 9.0 (June 2016): 6,125 ideographs, 755 components and an iteration mark, a sign that repeats the preceding character. Later versions added further ideographs and components. [3][5] Unicode gave the script code points, the numbers that identify each character, and fonts such as Noto Serif Tangut set it today. [5][11]
intro.close: The finders on this site look up a Tangut character by its shape, its sound or its meaning.
nav.eras.hint: Western Xia era names, titles and state names in Tangut
eras.intro: Click a character to open its record.
eras.coins.title: Coins
eras.coins.intro: The four characters run clockwise: top, right, bottom, left. 𘏨𘔭 means “precious coin”.
eras.coins.readings: Reconstructions: Li Fanwen, 夏漢字典 (1997), as quoted by West.
eras.coins.references: XHZD: 夏漢字典 (1997). WHYJ: 文海研究 (1983). Numbers follow West’s character table.
eras.coins.note.fusheng: Two readings of the same coin: Luo Fuchang’s 福聖 and Chen Bingying’s 稟德, as reported by West. West leaves the inscription unresolved.
eras.coins.note.zhenguan: West reads the first two characters as 德 and 觀, giving 觀德 in Chinese word order. He questions the attribution to 貞觀.
eras.coins.note.zhengde: The second character is uncertain. Bai Bin identifies 治德 with 正德; West questions that identification.
eras.contemporary.title: Contemporary Jin era
eras.contemporary.note: 西夏泉女——李子999 tentatively reads this privately held decorative object as 贞祐宝钱. Its authenticity, date and official status are uncertain.
eras.contemporary.comparison: Read counterclockwise from top to left, bottom and right; all four signs differ from standard forms.
eras.contemporary.dictionary: Clauson’s dictionary, West’s index and 夏漢字典 give 𘑨 for 祐; the left sign is probably a distorted 祐.
eras.doubt: Nie Hongyin (2004) says no Tangut form of this era was known.
eras.kind.coin.hint: Read on coins of the era, with a clear reading.
eras.kind.disputed.hint: Read on a coin, but the reading, or whether the coin names this era, is disputed.
eras.kind.calendar.hint: In West’s calendar, which names no source for its Tangut forms.
eras.kind.post.hint: In a post on X that names no source; it can differ from the calendar.
eras.kind.none.hint: None of the sources used here gives a Tangut form.
eras.gloss: The Tangut 貞觀政要 writes the Tang era 貞觀 with these two characters.
eras.posthumous.intro: Temple and posthumous names, and the names of tombs, as 宋史 records them, with the personal name of each ruler. 太祖 and 太宗 died before the state was proclaimed.
eras.posthumous.name: Personal name
eras.posthumous.zhaojian: A caption after 夏漢字典 gives these characters; in the 慈悲道場懺法 the same four close 惠宗's title, rendered 大明皇帝.
eras.posthumous.empresses.intro: Mothers and consorts of rulers, under the names 宋史 gives them. It does not say which of these are posthumous.
eras.states.intro: What the state was called, in Tangut and Chinese sources and in studies.
eras.states.note.xia: Chinese texts of the state use this form, as in a manuscript dated 乾祐, found by Kychanov and photographed by Kepping. She finds it in Tangut only after the state fell; the only example she knows is from 1312.
eras.states.note.bangni: 陳瑋 takes this as a transcription of the Tangut 白高國. It is also spelled 邦泥鼎, 邦尼定, 邦兒定 and 邦面令.
eras.states.note.mi: Kepping calls this the unofficial name, used in the Tangut Code.
eras.states.note.songs: Kepping says this is used in Tangut ritual songs. The Chinese comes from Wikipedia.
eras.states.note.baishang: Reads 𗴂𗹭 as "upper reaches of the White River", a reading Kepping rejects.
eras.later.intro: Four era names that match era names of the Yuan. Their Tangut forms come from a table posted without a source, and neither the table nor this site’s records say which dynasty they belong to.
eras.later.colophon: A Tangut colophon dated 大德四年 is reported in translation only.
eras.title: Names and titles of the Western Xia
eras.titles.intro: Titles of emperors, empresses dowager and forebears, as Tangut texts write them or as studies and Chinese histories give them. Chinese is quoted as each source prints it.
eras.titles.city.intro: Titles that contain 城 (𗍁), called city titles. Chinese Wikipedia, after 崔紅芬 and 文志勇, calls them a kind of Western Xia honorific that is still unexplained; some researchers take them as close to posthumous names.
eras.titles.basis.text.hint: The Tangut occurs in a text on this site.
eras.titles.basis.reported.hint: A source gives this Tangut; no text on this site confirms it.
eras.titles.basis.chinese.hint: Only Chinese is listed here. A study may print the Tangut in a font not decoded here.
eras.titles.caption: The holder rests on a Commons caption.
eras.titles.decoded: The holder rests on matching this string here with font codes in a study; no study states it.
eras.titles.codes: A study prints this title in font codes. The characters are worked out here from those codes and parallel texts; its source note gives the details and what stays uncertain.
eras.titles.disputed: The sources disagree on who held it.
eras.titles.dated: The holder is inferred from the date of the passage.
card.ccamcNote: Further readings and meanings are on CCAMC's page for this character.
reading.ccamcNote: CCAMC records this reading; the value stays on its page.
about.wiktionary: Five reconstructions, English and Japanese meanings, and variant forms come from Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0), with English entries extracted by Kaikki. Chinese meanings come from the Chinese Wiktionary dump of 2026-11-01, with each page's revision and contributor history recorded. Gong Hwang-cherng and Gong Xun 2024-11 come from the Tangut Pronunciation Database (DOI 10.25365/phaidra.654), cited per character.
about.readingsSource: Each Wiktionary reading comes from the module that renders it, fetched with its revision id and recorded in data/wiktionary/txg-readings.json.gz. Gong Hwang-cherng's GHC and Gong Xun's GX202411 are snapshotted from the 2025-05-07 table of the Tangut Pronunciation Database, with its digest, DOI and attribution, in data/gong-xun/ghc.json.gz and data/gong-xun/gx202411.json.gz. CCAMC's one further system and its Chinese glosses are kept only as normalized search terms in app/data/tangut-ccamc-index.json.gz; no page renders them.
about.wenhai: The 文海 (12th century) analyses the glyph in its entry; its Chinese text is public domain and shown where the 文海 carries the character.
intro.fig.golden: A detail of the Golden Light Sutra in Tangut, written in gold on indigo. 11th–13th century.
intro.fig.tombs: The Western Xia mausoleums at the foot of the Helan Mountains, near Yinchuan.
intro.fig.manuscript: A Tangut manuscript of Buddhist verses, found in the Helan Mountains and kept in the Ningxia Museum.
intro.fig.pearl: A page of the Pearl in the Palm (1190), the Tangut–Chinese glossary that records the sound of each Tangut character with Chinese characters.
intro.fig.khara: The stupas and walls of Khara-Khoto, where Pyotr Kozlov excavated Tangut manuscripts in 1909.
intro.fig.pillars: The two dharani pillars at Baoding, erected in 1502. Their Tangut text is the last dated use of the script.
intro.imageNote: The images are resized or cropped copies of the originals and remain under the licences named in their credits; each credit links to its source file.
